titles.Mucosa: Support tissue, vessels and thin muscle

Epithelium.description: The lining is a single layer of tall column-shaped cells. Most are absorptive enterocytes with a brush border of microvilli on their surface, and scattered goblet cells secrete mucus. At the base of the crypts, stem cells keep renewing the lining, and Paneth cells there release antibacterial granules.
clinical: In coeliac disease, an immune reaction to gluten flattens the villi and damages the enterocytes. The lining then absorbs less, so iron and fat-soluble vitamins are often poorly absorbed.
Lactase, an enzyme on the brush border, splits milk sugar. When it is low, lactose reaches the colon, where bacteria ferment it and cause bloating and diarrhoea.

Villi.description: Each villus is a small leaf-like fold of the mucosa with a core of loose connective tissue. The core holds a central lacteal that takes up absorbed fat, a capillary network that takes up sugars and amino acids, and smooth-muscle strands that can shorten the villus.
clinical: When the central lacteals are dilated, protein-rich lymph leaks into the gut. This causes low blood protein, swelling of the legs and diarrhoea.

Mucosa.description: The base of the mucosa is loose connective tissue called lamina propria, which fills the space between the crypts and carries lymphatic and small blood vessels. Its lowest layer is the muscularis mucosae, a thin sheet of smooth muscle that separates the mucosa from the submucosa and whose contraction helps fold the mucosa.

Submucosa.description: The submucosa is a layer of dense connective tissue between the mucosa and the muscle coat. In the duodenum it is packed with Brunner glands, which secrete alkaline mucus that neutralises stomach acid, and it carries the blood vessels and the submucosal (Meissner) nerve plexus.
clinical: A duodenal ulcer that erodes through the mucosa can open a blood vessel in the submucosa and cause bleeding. Ulcers on the back wall of the first part of the duodenum are the most likely to erode into the gastroduodenal artery and cause severe bleeding.
Brunner gland adenomas are rare, benign tumours that arise from these glands in the submucosa.

Muscularis externa.description: The muscularis externa is the muscle coat of the gut, with an inner circular layer and an outer longitudinal layer. Between them lies the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, a network of nerve ganglia that coordinates the waves of contraction called peristalsis.
clinical: In Chagas disease, a parasite infection destroys the myenteric plexus, so the gut muscle loses its coordination. The gut dilates most noticeably as megaoesophagus and megacolon.
This is a failure of the gut's nerve and muscle control, which causes obstruction-like symptoms even though nothing physically blocks the bowel.

Serosa.description: The serosa is a thin outer covering of simple squamous mesothelium over loose connective tissue, which keeps organ surfaces smooth and slippery. The first part of the duodenum sits in the peritoneal cavity and is covered by serosa, while the rest lies behind the peritoneum and has an adventitia instead.
clinical: A deep duodenal ulcer can perforate through every layer, including the serosa. Gut contents then spill into the abdomen and cause peritonitis, which is a surgical emergency.

parts.description: Villus enterocytes are the tall absorptive cells that line each villus, the small projections of the gut lining. Each one is a simple columnar cell standing on the basement membrane (the thin supporting layer beneath the epithelium), with an elongated nucleus near its base and a brush border of microvilli on its free surface. They absorb digested fats, sugars, amino acids and minerals into the blood and lymph. In a section, look for an unbroken layer of tall cells with a striped top edge along each villus.

Surface enterocytes are the tall absorptive cells that line the gut surface between the villi and at the openings of the crypts. They are simple columnar epithelial cells, like those on the villi, with a brush border of microvilli on their free surface. In a section, look for an unbroken sheet of tall cells with their nuclei near the base; the sheet dips down into each crypt opening.

Crypt epithelial cells are the cells lining the intestinal crypts (crypts of Lieberkühn), the narrow glands that open between the villi. The crypt population is less mature than the villus population: it includes stem cells, the dividing cells they produce, Paneth cells, goblet cells and enteroendocrine cells (hormone-producing cells). Most newly made cells migrate up onto the villi, where they mature into absorptive and other functional cells. In a section, the crypts look like short, narrow pits in the lining.

Goblet cell mucin is the secretory product that fills the cup-shaped upper part of each goblet cell. Mucins are large glycoproteins (proteins carrying many sugar chains) that swell into a slippery gel once released, lubricating the surface and protecting it from mechanical and chemical damage. In routine haematoxylin and eosin sections the mucin is largely lost during processing, so the cup looks pale and empty, whereas periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) or Alcian blue staining shows it clearly.

Paneth cells are specialised secretory cells found at the bottom of the small-intestinal crypts, between the stem cells. Each one is pyramid-shaped, with a broad base on the basement membrane and a cluster of large, acidophilic (pink-staining) granules at its apex facing the crypt lumen. Their secretions help control bacteria in the gut, and the cells also support the nearby stem cells. In a section, look for cells with bright pink-red granules at the very bottom of a crypt.

Paneth cell granules are the large, dense secretory granules packed into the apical (upper, lumen-facing) part of each Paneth cell. They are strongly acidophilic (eosinophilic), so in haematoxylin and eosin sections they look bright pink to red. The granules contain lysozyme (an enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls), defensins and other antimicrobial peptides, which are released by exocytosis into the crypt lumen. In a section, look for the pink granules crowding the top of each cell at the crypt base.

Crypt stem cells are the undifferentiated cells at the base of each intestinal crypt, lying between the Paneth cells. Their daughter cells, called transit-amplifying cells (progenitors that divide several more times), mostly move upwards and differentiate into enterocytes and goblet cells, while Paneth cells migrate down to the crypt base. This renewal replaces the whole lining roughly every three to five days. They are small, slender columnar cells with scanty cytoplasm, best recognised as the narrow cells wedged among the Paneth cells at the very bottom of the crypt.

The brush border is the dense layer of microvilli, tiny finger-like extensions of the cell membrane, on the free surface of each enterocyte. Microvilli greatly increase the absorptive area of the gut, and their membranes carry digestive enzymes such as disaccharidases and peptidases that finish breaking down food. In a section it appears as a dense, pink, fringe-like band along the top of the cells, which is why it is also called the striated border.

Epithelial nuclei are the nuclei of the lining cells of the mucosa, including enterocytes, goblet cells, Paneth cells and stem cells. Because the epithelium is a single layer, its nuclei form a fairly regular row near the base of the cells; enterocyte nuclei are elongated or oval. In haematoxylin and eosin sections they stain dark blue-purple, so this row of nuclei is an easy feature to recognise.

The villus core is the central column of loose connective tissue (lamina propria) that fills each villus and carries its blood and lymph vessels. It holds the central lacteal, the capillary network, the arteriole and venule, and a few smooth-muscle strands running up from the muscularis mucosae. The duodenal villi are broad and leaf-like, so their cores are wide; in a section the core looks pale pink with scattered cells and many small vessels.

A central lacteal is the blind-ended lymphatic capillary running up the middle of each villus. Its wall is a single layer of thin, flattened endothelial cells, and it takes up absorbed fat from the enterocytes as chylomicrons (fat droplets coated with protein and phospholipid). Its lymph, called chyle, looks milky in life, and it drains into the lymphatic plexus at the base of the mucosa. In a section it is a wide, pale, empty-looking channel in the centre of the villus, because processing dissolves the fat it carried.

The villus arteriole is a small muscular artery that reaches the villus from the deeper layers of the gut wall and runs up the centre of the villus core. Along its length it gives off branches that form the capillary network just beneath the epithelium. Its wall is thicker and more muscular than that of the venule beside it, which is how it is told apart in a section.

The villus venule is a thin-walled vein in the core of each villus that drains the capillary network. Blood leaving it carries the sugars and amino acids absorbed by the enterocytes, and it passes on to the submucosal venules and so to the hepatic portal vein. In a section, it is a rounded, thin-walled vessel with a relatively wide lumen, usually lying close to the villus arteriole.

The villus capillary network is the dense mesh of fenestrated capillaries lying just beneath the epithelial basement membrane. Blood enters it from the villus arteriole and leaves through the villus venule, and the fenestrations (small pores closed by a thin diaphragm) let absorbed sugars and amino acids pass quickly into the blood. In a section, it appears as a close net of small, red-cell-filled channels between the epithelium and the core.

The villus smooth muscle strands are bundles of smooth-muscle fibres that rise from the muscularis mucosae up into the core of each villus. Their fibres run lengthwise, and when they contract they shorten the villus and squeeze the central lacteal, which helps push absorbed fat along into the lymphatics. In a section, look for pink, elongated bands of muscle running from the base of the villus towards its tip.

Villus smooth-muscle cells are the individual spindle-shaped muscle cells that make up the strands in the villus core. Each cell is long and tapers at both ends, with a single central, cigar-shaped nucleus and pink, fibrillar cytoplasm. They lie parallel to the long axis of the villus, so in a longitudinal section they appear as elongated pink cells packed in bundles.

Villus fibroblasts are the connective-tissue cells of the villus core that make collagen fibres and the ground substance of the lamina propria. They are star-shaped or spindle-shaped, with slender branching processes and an oval, pale-staining nucleus. They are scattered through the loose matrix of the villus, and in a section they are told apart from smooth-muscle cells by their paler, less elongated nuclei.

Stromal cell nuclei are the nuclei of the supporting connective-tissue (stromal) cells of the villus core, mainly smooth-muscle cells and fibroblasts. Smooth-muscle nuclei are dark, elongated and rod-shaped, lying along the strands, whereas fibroblast nuclei are paler, oval and more loosely scattered through the matrix. Comparing nuclear shape is a useful way to tell the two cell types apart in a section.

The lamina propria is the layer of loose connective tissue directly beneath the surface epithelium. It fills the core of each villus and the spaces between the crypts, and it contains fibroblasts, lymphocytes, plasma cells, mast cells and eosinophils along with small blood and lymphatic vessels. It supports the epithelium, carries the blood and lymph vessels that feed it, and houses the immune cells that defend the gut lining. Its lower border is the muscularis mucosae, a thin layer of smooth muscle.

The mucosal lymphatic vessels are the lymph channels of the lamina propria that collect lymph from the central lacteals of the villi. The lacteals drain into a plexus of lymphatic vessels near the base of the mucosa, beside the muscularis mucosae, and lymph passes from there into the submucosal lymphatics. Their walls are thin, lined by a single layer of endothelium, and in a section they look pale and empty, containing lymph rather than red blood cells.

The muscularis mucosae is the thin layer of smooth muscle at the base of the mucosa, lying between the lamina propria above and the submucosa below. Its fibres run in an inner circular and an outer longitudinal sublayer, and its contraction changes the shape of the mucosal surface and helps move the villi. Brunner gland ducts pierce it on their way to the crypts, and in a section it appears as a thin, pink band of smooth muscle with elongated nuclei.

Mucosal arterial branches are the small arteries and arterioles that climb from the submucosa, pass through the muscularis mucosae and carry blood up to the villi. There they break up into the capillary network of each villus, which nourishes the lamina propria and the epithelium above it. In a section, they look like small, thick-walled vessels with a round lumen in the lamina propria beneath the villi.

Mucosal venous branches are the small veins that drain blood from the capillary network of each villus and carry it down through the mucosa to the submucosal venule. Their walls are thin and their lumens are wider than those of the arterial branches that run beside them. In a section, look for thin-walled vessels with a wide, irregular lumen in the lamina propria near the base of the mucosa.

Submucosal connective tissue is the dense, irregular connective tissue of the submucosa, the layer between the mucosa and the muscularis externa. It carries the larger blood vessels and lymphatics, the submucosal (Meissner) plexus and, in the duodenum, the Brunner glands. In a section, it looks like a pink-staining layer of collagen fibres running in many directions, with scattered fibroblast nuclei.

Brunner gland mucous cells are the pale secretory cells that line the acini of Brunner's glands in the duodenal submucosa. Their mucin-filled cytoplasm stains pale, so the cells look clear or foamy in a section. They secrete an alkaline, bicarbonate-rich mucus that neutralises acid from the stomach and protects the duodenal wall, and their presence in the submucosa identifies the duodenum.

Brunner gland duct cells are the cuboidal cells that line the short excretory ducts of Brunner's glands. The ducts climb from the submucosa through the muscularis mucosae and open into the base of the intestinal crypts, carrying the alkaline secretion of the glands with them. In a section, look for small lumens lined by cells that are smaller and more regular than the pale mucous cells of the acini around them.

Brunner gland nuclei are the nuclei of the mucous cells that make up the secretory acini of Brunner's glands in the submucosa. Mucin fills each cell, so the nucleus is pushed to its base and flattened into a dark, crescent-shaped or disc-like profile. In a section, look for these flat, dark nuclei squeezed against the base of the pale cells of the acini.

The submucosal arteriole is a small artery of the submucosa, with a thick smooth-muscle wall around a small, round lumen. It supplies the branches that climb through the muscularis mucosae to the villi, and it helps regulate local blood flow to the mucosa. In a section, look for the thick muscular wall and small, round lumen, which distinguish the arteriole from the thin-walled submucosal venule beside it.

The submucosal venule is a small vein of the submucosa that collects blood from the mucosal venous branches and drains it towards larger submucosal veins. Its wall is thin, with little smooth muscle, and its lumen is wider than that of the companion arteriole. Pick out the venule in a section by its thin wall and wide lumen beside a thick-walled arteriole.

The submucosal (Meissner's) plexus is a network of small enteric ganglia and nerve strands lying in the submucosa, between the mucosa and the inner circular muscle. It is part of the enteric nervous system, and it controls gland secretion, local blood flow and absorption in the mucosa, largely independently of the brain. In a section, look for small clusters of neurons with large, pale nuclei in the submucosa.

The inner circular muscle is the inner layer of smooth muscle in the muscularis externa, lying between the submucosa and the myenteric plexus. Its fibres wrap around the gut, so their contraction narrows the lumen and helps push contents along in peristalsis. In a transverse section of the wall, its cells are cut lengthwise and look like long, spindle-shaped strands.

Circular muscle nuclei are the nuclei of the smooth muscle cells in the inner circular layer of the muscularis externa. Each nucleus is elongated and cigar-shaped, lying near the centre of a spindle-shaped cell. Because the circular fibres are cut lengthwise in a transverse section, these nuclei appear as long, rod-like profiles, unlike the round nuclei of the enteric neurons.

The myenteric connective septum is the thin sheet of loose connective tissue that lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle layers. It holds the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, the ganglia and nerve strands that run between the two layers, and small blood vessels pass through it to supply the muscle. In a section, it appears as a pale, fibrous band with scattered fibroblast nuclei between the two bands of smooth muscle.

The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus is a network of enteric ganglia and nerve strands lying between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle layers. It mainly controls gut motility, coordinating peristalsis and the rhythmic contraction of the muscle layers. In a section, look for clusters of ganglion cells with large, pale nuclei in the connective tissue between the two muscle layers.

Myenteric ganglion neurons are the nerve cells whose bodies make up the ganglia of the myenteric plexus. They are multipolar, with several dendrites and one axon, and include motor neurons that drive the muscle layers and interneurons that link the ganglia. Their cell bodies are surrounded by satellite glial cells, and in a section they appear as large, rounded cells with prominent nucleoli.

Myenteric neuron nuclei are the nuclei of the enteric neurons inside the myenteric ganglia. They are large, round and pale, with open (vesicular) chromatin and a prominent nucleolus, so they stand out from the small, dark, elongated nuclei of the smooth muscle and glial cells around them. Look for round, pale profiles grouped in the ganglia between the two muscle layers.

The outer longitudinal muscle is the outer layer of smooth muscle in the muscularis externa, lying just beneath the serosa and outside the myenteric plexus. Its fibres run parallel to the length of the gut, so their contraction shortens the segment of gut. In a transverse section of the wall, its fibres are cut across, so the cells look like small, round or oval profiles in a band just inside the serosa.

Longitudinal muscle nuclei are the nuclei of the smooth muscle cells in the outer longitudinal layer of the muscularis externa. Because these cells run along the length of the gut, a transverse section cuts across them, so their nuclei look small and round or oval. Compare them with the long, rod-like nuclei of the inner circular layer, which are cut lengthwise in the same section.

Serosal connective tissue is the thin layer of loose areolar connective tissue that lies directly beneath the mesothelium of the serosa. It carries small blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves to the outer wall of the gut and anchors the mesothelium to the muscularis externa below. In a section, it appears as a pale, loosely arranged band of collagen and elastic fibres with scattered fibroblasts beneath the flat surface cells.

Mesothelium is the single layer of flat, squamous cells that forms the smooth, glistening surface of the serosa. It is continuous with the peritoneum lining the abdominal cavity, and it secretes a thin film of serous fluid that lets the bowel slide easily against neighbouring organs. In a section, look for a single, unbroken line of very flat cells resting on a thin basement membrane.

Mesothelial nuclei are the flat, oval nuclei of the squamous mesothelial cells that form the surface of the serosa. The cells are so thin that their nuclei are the most visible part of each cell, and they bulge slightly above the surface line in a section. Look for one nucleus per cell, spaced in an even row along the surface.
